hooks: From Bauzanum, a Roman estate name; in German it is Bozen, and both are official here.
About 70% of the province speaks German as its first language, and a quarter of all Italian apples are grown in its valleys.
Ötzi, the 5,300-year-old iceman found in a glacier on its border in 1991, is kept in a refrigerated cell in the town museum.
Probably from Lombard sondrio, a lord’s demesne farm, from an older Germanic word.
The Valtellina here is terraced for nebbiolo on slopes so steep the wine is called heroic viticulture.
Its bresaola, air-dried beef, has protected status, and the Stelvio pass above it has 48 hairpins.
From Celtic belo-dunum, "bright hill fort" — dunum is the same element as in London and Lyon.
The Dolomites here are a UNESCO site, pale limestone that turns pink at sunset in the effect called enrosadira.
The 1963 Vajont dam disaster in this province killed about 2,000 people when a landslide pushed the reservoir over the dam.
Possibly from a pre-Roman word for a height, or from Udene, an old settlement name.
The capital of Friuli, where Friulian is spoken — a Romance language in its own right, not an Italian dialect.
Its castle hill is said to have been raised by Attila’s men so he could watch Aquileia burn.
From Tridentum, "three teeth", for the three peaks above it — the city’s symbol is still a trident.
The Council of Trent met here from 1545 to 1563 and defined the Catholic response to the Reformation.
Its MUSE science museum was designed by Renzo Piano, and the province makes most of Italy’s metodo classico sparkling wine.
Three names in one: Verbano is the Latin name of Lake Maggiore, Cusio of Lake Orta, and Ossola the alpine valley above them.
Created only in 1992, one of Italy’s newest provinces.
The Borromean islands in its lake hold baroque gardens built on terraces over the water.
From Portus Naonis, "the port on the Noncello" — it was a river port before the water level dropped.
Its silent film festival is the most important in the world for early cinema.
The province was created in 1968, split from Udine.
From Comum, a pre-Roman name of unclear meaning; Caesar settled colonists here in 59 BC.
Alessandro Volta was born here and invented the battery; the volt is named after him and there is a temple to him on the lakefront.
Its silk industry has woven for Paris and Milan since the 1500s.
Possibly from Latin leucus or a Celtic word for a lake or a stone.
Manzoni set The Betrothed here, the novel that did most to shape modern literary Italian.
Split from Como in 1992, and its Grigne mountains are where Italian alpinism was invented.
From Slovene gorica, "little hill" — the town sits under one.
The border with Slovenia ran straight through the city from 1947; Nova Gorica was built on the other side, and the two were joint European Capital of Culture in 2025.
The Isonzo front here saw twelve battles in the First World War and hundreds of thousands of casualties.
Of uncertain origin, possibly from a pre-Roman root or from Latin varicia.
Called the garden city for its villas and parks, and the Sacro Monte above it is a UNESCO site.
Italy’s shoe and aviation industries both have roots here; Agusta helicopters are built in the province.
From Tarvisium, probably Celtic tarvos, "bull".
Prosecco comes mainly from its hills at Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, a UNESCO landscape.
Radicchio and tiramisù are both claimed by this province, the second with reasonable evidence from a restaurant in the town.
From Brixia, from a Celtic word for a hill.
Its Roman forum and Lombard monastery complex are a UNESCO site, and the Winged Victory bronze found here is its emblem.
The Mille Miglia road race has started and finished here since 1927.
From Bergomum, probably Celtic or Ligurian, from a root meaning mountain.
Its Città Alta sits inside Venetian walls that are a UNESCO site, reached by funicular from the lower town.
Donizetti was born here, and the province was the hardest hit place in Europe in the first wave of the 2020 pandemic.
From Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, founded in 25 BC and named for Augustus — Aosta is Augusta worn down.
Its Roman gate and theatre still stand, and the street plan is the original grid.
French is co-official, Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn are both on its borders, and it is the smallest and least populated region in Italy.
From Tergeste, probably from a pre-Roman root terg, a market.
It was Austria’s only major port for five centuries, which is why it has Viennese coffee houses and a Habsburg waterfront.
Joyce lived here for eleven years and wrote much of Ulysses in the city, and Svevo was his English pupil.
Monza is from Modicia, of unknown origin; Brianza is probably from a Celtic word for a highland.
Its autodrome has hosted the Italian Grand Prix since 1922 and is the fastest circuit in Formula One.
The Iron Crown of Lombardy, said to contain a nail from the Crucifixion, is kept in Monza cathedral.
From Vicetia, probably from Latin vicus, a village.
Palladio built more than twenty buildings here, and the city is a UNESCO site for them.
His Teatro Olimpico of 1585 is the oldest surviving indoor theatre in the world, with a permanent perspective stage set.
From Novaria — nov is new and aria probably a Celtic word for a plain.
It grows more rice than anywhere else in Europe, flooded paddies that mirror the Alps in spring.
The Basilica di San Gaudenzio’s dome, 121 m, is one of the tallest brick structures in the world.
Of uncertain, probably Celtic, origin.
The centre of Italian wool: Zegna, Cerruti and Loro Piana all began here, using soft Alpine water for washing fleece.
The Sanctuary of Oropa above it is the largest Marian sanctuary in the Alps and a UNESCO site.
From Vercellae, probably Celtic ver-cella, "high dwelling".
It has Europe’s largest rice-growing area, and the Vercelli Book here holds some of the oldest Old English poetry in existence — nobody knows how it got to Italy.
Its basilica of Sant’Andrea from 1219 is one of the first Gothic buildings in Italy.
Of uncertain origin, possibly Etruscan or from a Celtic personal name.
Its Roman arena from 30 AD still stages opera to 15,000 people, and the city is a UNESCO site.
Shakespeare set Romeo and Juliet here without ever visiting; the balcony was added to a medieval house in the 1930s.
From the Veneti, the pre-Roman people of the region.
The city is built on about 118 islands on millions of wooden piles, and was an independent republic for 1,100 years.
Marco Polo, Vivaldi and Casanova were all Venetians, and the city has no roads at all in its historic centre.
From Mediolanum, "in the middle of the plain" — medio plus a Celtic word for a plain.
Leonardo painted the Last Supper here, on a wall that has been deteriorating since he finished it in 1498.
It is Italy’s financial capital and one of the world’s four fashion capitals, and its Duomo took nearly six centuries to build.
From Patavium, possibly from a root meaning a marsh or a ford.
Its university, founded 1222, is the second oldest in Italy; Galileo taught here for eighteen years and called them his happiest.
Giotto’s Scrovegni Chapel frescoes of 1305 are a UNESCO site and effectively begin Western painting.
From Laus Pompeia, "the praise of Pompeius", after a Roman consul — the modern town was founded by Barbarossa in 1158 after the old one was destroyed.
Its grana padano and mascarpone come from the same dairy plain.
Napoleon’s victory at the bridge of Lodi in 1796 made his reputation at twenty-six.
A Roman colony of 218 BC; the name may be Celtic or Etruscan.
Stradivari, Amati and Guarneri all worked here, and the town still makes violins by hand in about 150 workshops.
Its 112 m Torrazzo is one of the tallest brick bell towers in the world, with the largest astronomical clock.
From Mantus, an Etruscan god of the underworld, by the usual account.
The Gonzaga ruled it for four centuries and commissioned Mantegna’s Camera degli Sposi; the city is a UNESCO site.
Virgil was born just outside it, and it is surrounded on three sides by artificial lakes dug in the 1100s.
From Augusta Taurinorum — the Taurini were the local Celtic-Ligurian people, and the bull on the city arms is a pun on their name.
It was the first capital of united Italy, from 1861 to 1865, and Fiat was founded here in 1899.
Its Mole Antonelliana, built as a synagogue and now the film museum, was the tallest brick building in the world.
From Ticinum, renamed Papia in the Lombard period, which wore down to Pavia.
It was the capital of the Lombard kingdom, and its university was founded in 1361.
The Certosa di Pavia, a Carthusian monastery of extraordinary marble facade, was begun in 1396 as a Visconti mausoleum.
Of uncertain origin, possibly from Rhodigium, itself perhaps from a personal name.
The Polesine, the land between the Adige and the Po, is largely below sea level and was catastrophically flooded in 1951.
The Po delta here is a UNESCO biosphere and Italy’s largest wetland.
Founded in 1168 and named for Pope Alexander III, as a fortress against Barbarossa.
It has made most of Italy’s hats — Borsalino was founded here in 1857.
Marengo nearby gave Napoleon his 1800 victory and a chicken dish its name.
From Placentia, "the pleasing place", founded as a Roman colony in 218 BC.
The Liver of Piacenza, a bronze sheep’s liver marked with Etruscan god names, is the key artefact for understanding Etruscan divination.
It stands where the Via Emilia begins, and its two bronze equestrian statues by Mochi are among the finest of the baroque.
From Hasta, probably a Ligurian word for a height.
Asti spumante and moscato come from its hills, a UNESCO wine landscape shared with Langhe and Monferrato.
Its Palio, a bareback horse race, is older than Siena’s and has run since at least 1275.
Possibly from ferrum, iron, or from a word for a ferry crossing on the Po.
The Este dukes made it a Renaissance capital, and its 1492 town extension is considered the first modern urban plan in Europe.
It is a UNESCO site, and the whole city is ringed by nine kilometres of walls you can cycle on.
Probably from an Etruscan or Ligurian word, or from the Latin for a round shield.
Parmigiano Reggiano and prosciutto di Parma are both from here and both protected.
Correggio painted its cathedral dome, Verdi was born in the province, and Toscanini in the city.
From Regium Lepidi, founded by the consul Aemilius Lepidus who also built the Via Emilia.
The Italian tricolour was first adopted here in 1797, in a hall now called the Sala del Tricolore.
Its Reggio Emilia approach to early childhood education is followed in schools worldwide.
From Mutina, probably Etruscan.
Ferrari, Maserati, Lamborghini, De Tomaso and Pagani are all built within a few kilometres of the city.
Its cathedral and Ghirlandina tower are a UNESCO site, and traditional balsamic vinegar is aged here for at least twelve years.
Italian for "wedge" — the town sits on a wedge of land between two rivers.
Its Langhe and Roero hills are a UNESCO wine landscape, producing Barolo and Barbaresco.
The white truffles of Alba here are the most expensive food on earth by weight.
Possibly from a Ligurian root genu, a knee or a mouth — the bend of its harbour.
Columbus was born here, and the republic of Genoa ran a trading empire from Crimea to Gibraltar.
Its Rolli palaces are a UNESCO site, and pesto, focaccia and the jeans fabric named for Gênes all come from the city.
From Bononia, a Celtic Boii settlement Latinised — the Boii also named Bohemia.
Its university, founded 1088, is the oldest continuously operating one in the world.
It has about 38 km of arcaded porticoes, a UNESCO site, and is nicknamed la dotta, la grassa, la rossa — learned, fat and red.
Of uncertain, possibly Etruscan or Umbrian, origin.
It was capital of the Western Roman Empire, then of the Ostrogoths, then of Byzantine Italy.
Its eight early Christian buildings hold the finest mosaics in the world and are a UNESCO site; Dante is buried here.
From Savo, a Ligurian settlement name.
Three popes came from the town, and Columbus’s father owned land in the province.
Its coast is the Riviera delle Palme, and the port is now one of the Mediterranean’s main cruise terminals.
Probably from Latin spedia or a word for a spice warehouse — the derivation is contested.
The Cinque Terre are in this province: five villages on terraced cliffs, a UNESCO site, reachable for centuries only by boat or footpath.
Shelley drowned in its gulf in 1822, which is why it is called the Gulf of Poets.
Massa is from a Latin word for a landed estate; Carrara is probably from a Celtic-Ligurian word for stone.
Carrara marble has been quarried for over two thousand years — the Pantheon, Michelangelo’s David and Marble Arch are all made of it.
Michelangelo came here himself to choose blocks, and some quarries he opened are still worked.
Forlì is from Forum Livii, the market of Livius; Cesena from Caesena, probably Etruscan.
The Malatesta Library in Cesena is the only surviving example of a European humanist monastic library still in its original building with its original furniture and books.
It is a UNESCO Memory of the World site, and the books are still chained to the desks.
Probably from Ligurian luk, a marshy place, or a Celtic word for a wood.
Its Renaissance walls survive completely intact and are now a tree-lined park circling the city.
It was an independent republic for nearly five centuries, and Puccini was born here.
From Pistoriae, possibly from pistor, a baker.
The pistol is said by one theory to be named after the town, which made small firearms.
Its nurseries grow a large share of Europe’s ornamental plants, and the cathedral has a silver altar worked on for two centuries.
From Ariminum, named for the river Ariminus.
Its Arch of Augustus from 27 BC is the oldest surviving Roman arch, and the Tiberius bridge still carries traffic after two thousand years.
Fellini was born here, and the coast invented the Italian package beach holiday.
The newest name on the map: invented in 1923 when Porto Maurizio and Oneglia were merged, after the river Impero.
It produces the taggiasca olive, whose oil is the most prized in Liguria.
Sanremo in the province has held Italy’s song festival since 1951, which is where the Eurovision Song Contest came from.
Italian for "meadow" — the field the town grew on.
It has been a textile city since the Middle Ages and pioneered recycling wool from rags.
It has one of the largest Chinese communities in Europe, working in its garment trade, and was made a province only in 1992.
From Florentia, "flourishing" — a Roman colony of 59 BC for Caesar’s veterans.
The Renaissance began here: Brunelleschi’s dome, still the largest masonry dome in the world, was raised without a supporting framework.
Its dialect became standard Italian because Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio all wrote in it.
